tagline: Across the emigrant trails, from coal town to sheep town.
intro: Leaving Kemmerer, the backway turns onto a dirt track and runs 68 miles to Cokeville, crossing old emigrant trails, following willowed river valleys and plunging deep into the Tunp Range of the Bridger National Forest. Abandoned homesteads stand within sight of the road.
Between 1841 and 1868 more than 350,000 emigrants crossed this part of the country with loaded wagons, bound for Utah, Oregon and California. In places their wagon ruts still show.

moments.title: Kemmerer
moments.text: James Cash Penney opened his first Golden Rule Store here in 1902, in a coal town only five years old, and it became the start of the J. C. Penney chain.

moments.title: Old Settler Cabin
moments.text: The first of the abandoned homesteads is the Old Settler Cabin, a sagging log structure out on a windswept plain.

moments.title: Cokeville
moments.text: Named for the coal found nearby, the town turned to sheep after the railroad came, and at the peak, in 1918, it was known, informally, as the Sheep Capital of the World.

practical: An unimproved Forest Service road through very remote country that calls for excellent map navigation. Four-wheel drive is highly recommended, and the Forest Service recommends only high-clearance vehicles west of Kelley Guard Station.
